passages.t: A shut city and a strange plan
passages.happening:
“Now Jericho was tightly shut up because of the Israelites. No one went out and no one came in” (verse 1).

The LORD speaks to Joshua as if the matter were already settled: “Behold, I have delivered Jericho into your hand, along with its king and its mighty men of valor” (verse 2).

Then he gives the plan. The fighting men are to walk around the city once a day for six days. Seven priests are to carry seven rams' horns in front of the ark. On the seventh day they are to go around seven times, with the priests blowing the horns. At a long blast the people are to give a great shout. “Then the wall of the city will collapse and all your people will charge straight into the city” (verse 5).

Joshua passes the orders on to the priests and the people (verses 6-7).
passages.hearers:
Jericho had shut its gates. Rahab had said that the city's courage was gone, and this verse shows it. It was a walled town with a strong spring of its own.

An army of that time would have settled down to a siege. God commands nothing of the kind. He tells Israel to walk and to blow horns. The plan makes no sense as a siege. It makes sense only as an act of trust in what God had said in verse 2: ‘I have delivered Jericho into your hand’. The city is given before anyone moves.

The ram's horn, in Hebrew the shofar, was not a musical instrument in the usual sense. It was a signal horn. It called people together, sounded alarms, and announced holy days. The ark was the sign of God's presence. So the thing that circles Jericho looks less like an army and more like a procession of worship, with priests, horns and the ark at its center.

The number seven runs all through the plan: seven priests, seven horns, seven days, seven circuits on the seventh day. In the Bible seven is the number of completeness and of God's own work, as in the seven days of creation.

A reader should know that the remains of ancient Jericho have been dug several times and that archaeologists disagree about what they show. Most hold that the last great walled city there fell long before any date proposed for Joshua. Others have argued for a later date. The mound is badly eroded. The book page sets out each view and takes no side.
passages.later:
The New Testament remembers this chapter for one thing, the people's trust: “By faith the walls of Jericho fell, after the people had marched around them for seven days” (Hebrews 11:30).

A psalm says what the plan was meant to teach: “Some trust in chariots and others in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God” (Psalm 20:7).
passages.asks: God said ‘I have delivered’ before a single step was taken, and then gave orders that looked foolish. Ask what God has asked of you that seems too small or too odd to matter. And ask what you reach for first when something stands in your way: your own strength and cleverness, or what God has said.

passages.t: Six silent days, and the seventh
passages.happening:
The procession sets out. Armed men go first. Seven priests follow, blowing the horns. The ark comes after them, and a rear guard behind it (verses 8-9).

Joshua has given the people one more order: “Do not give a battle cry or let your voice be heard; do not let one word come out of your mouth until the day I tell you to shout” (verse 10).

They walk around the city once and go back to camp for the night. The next day they do the same. “They did this for six days” (verse 14).

On the seventh day they rise at dawn and go around seven times. After the seventh circuit the priests blow the horns, and Joshua gives the word: “Shout! For the LORD has given you the city!” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The writer tells this slowly on purpose. He repeats the order of march again and again: troops, priests, horns, ark, rear guard, back to camp. The reader is made to walk the circuit with Israel and to feel how long six days is when nothing seems to happen.

The silence would have been hard. A battle cry gave an army its courage. Israel is told to say nothing for six days. The people had only the sound of the horns and the sight of the ark.

Each day they went back to camp with the wall still standing. Nothing in the plan gave them a sign along the way. Obedience on the fourth day looked exactly like obedience on the first.

When the shout comes, it is tied to a statement of fact. Joshua does not say that God will give the city if they shout loudly enough. He says God ‘has given’ it. The shout is the people's answer to a gift already made. The Hebrew word for this shout is used in the Psalms for the glad cry of worship as well as for a battle cry.
passages.later:
The Psalms call for a glad shout of the same kind in worship: “Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth” (Psalm 100:1).

Paul takes up the language of pulling down walls and gives it a wholly different object. “The weapons of our warfare are not the weapons of the world. Instead, they have divine power to demolish strongholds. We tear down arguments and every presumption set up against the knowledge of God” (2 Corinthians 10:4-5). The strongholds the church is sent against are not cities and not people.
passages.asks: For six days Israel obeyed and saw no change at all. Ask where you are on the third or fourth day of something God has asked of you, with the wall still standing. Ask what it would take to walk the circuit again tomorrow. And ask whether you can keep silent when you most want to speak, if silence is what faithfulness asks.

passages.happening:
Before the people shout, Joshua gives three orders.

The first is the ban. “Now the city and everything in it must be devoted to the LORD for destruction” (verse 17).

The second is an exception. “Only Rahab the prostitute and all those with her in her house will live, because she hid the spies we sent” (verse 17).

The third is a warning to Israel. No one is to take anything for himself. “But keep away from the things devoted to destruction, lest you yourself be set apart for destruction” (verse 18). The silver and gold and the vessels of bronze and iron belong to the LORD and go into his treasury (verse 19).

Then the horns sound, the people shout, and the wall collapses. The people go straight in and take the city (verse 20).

The next verse says what was done, and it has to be quoted. ‘At the edge of the sword they devoted to destruction everything in the city’ (verse 21). It names man and woman, young and old, and the animals.
passages.hearers:
The phrase ‘devoted to destruction’ translates one Hebrew word, herem. It is often called the ban. Something under the ban was given over wholly to God and taken out of human use. In war it meant that the people of a city were killed, and that its goods were destroyed or handed to the sanctuary. The victors kept nothing.

Israel did not invent the ban. A king of Moab named Mesha set up a monument in the ninth century BC on which he boasts that he devoted an Israelite town to his own god, and he uses the same word. It was known across the region.

In Israel's law the ban on the cities of Canaan came with a stated reason, and the reason was worship. They were to be devoted ‘so that they cannot teach you to do all the detestable things they do for their gods’ (Deuteronomy 20:18). The law names the worst of those things: “They even burn their sons and daughters in the fire as sacrifices to their gods” (Deuteronomy 12:31).

The ban also shut out greed. An ordinary army fought for plunder: goods, animals and captives. At Jericho no soldier was to gain anything. That is why Joshua warns Israel so sharply. A man who takes what is under the ban brings the ban on himself and on the camp. The next chapter shows that the warning was meant.

So the same order that dooms a Canaanite city holds a Canaanite household safe and threatens any Israelite who breaks it. The line in this chapter is not drawn by birth.

None of this makes verse 21 easy, and a reader should not pretend that it does. The verse is short and it does not linger. These notes will not linger over it either. But they will not look away from the words ‘young and old’.

From the early church onward some preachers, Origen among them, also read these wars as a picture of the believer's fight against sin. That reading stands beside the others. It does not answer the question of what was done at Jericho.
passages.later:
The command came from the law of Moses: “However, in the cities of the nations that the LORD your God is giving you as an inheritance, you must not leave alive anything that breathes” (Deuteronomy 20:16).

The same law speaks of the peoples of the land being moved out slowly: “Little by little I will drive them out ahead of you” (Exodus 23:30). And late in this book God says to Joshua that ‘very much of the land remains to be possessed’ (Joshua 13:1).

Jesus, in the same land many centuries later, commanded, “love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44). When two disciples wanted to call down fire on a village, “Jesus turned and rebuked them” (Luke 9:55).
passages.hard:
How can God command the destruction of a whole city, with its women and children?

This is one of the hardest places in the Bible. The verse says ‘young and old’, and nothing in these notes softens that. A reader who is grieved by it is reading with a conscience the Bible formed: “Fathers shall not be put to death for their children, nor children for their fathers” (Deuteronomy 24:16).

Christians who receive this book as God's word read the chapter in several ways, as the site's pages on the conquest set out. Each has a cost.

Some read it as judgment on named evil after long patience (Genesis 15:16; Deuteronomy 9:5). The cost is the children, for whom this reading has no answer that takes the grief away.

Some read the language of total destruction as the stock idiom of ancient war, which this book itself qualifies, since Canaanites are still in the land in later chapters and in Judges. The cost is that this eases the scale and not the substance.

Some ground it in God's unique right over life, as Augustine and Thomas Aquinas did. The cost is that it does not show how anyone could know such a command was God's.

Some read these texts as God stooping to the understanding of an ancient people, to be seen through Christ. The cost is that the reader must decide which portraits of God to trust, and critics say this weakens the authority of Scripture.

Many hold more than one together. The site takes no side, and none of them makes the chapter easy.

Under all of them these things hold. The ban was tied to one land and one moment, and it was never renewed. It was not about race: a Canaanite family is saved in this chapter, and an Israelite falls under the same ban in the next. The New Testament gives the church no city to take.

So it must be said plainly. No one may use this chapter to justify violence against any person or people. The people of Jericho passed away long ago. The chapter says nothing about any nation, state, land or conflict today. Christians did later quote such chapters over their own wars. That was a misuse of the text, and the church must own it as sin.

Nothing here permits contempt for the people of Jericho or for anyone. God says, “Do I take any pleasure in the death of the wicked?” (Ezekiel 18:23).

The site's pages on the violence of the Old Testament and on the command to destroy the Canaanites go further.
passages.asks: This is a passage to be honest with. Ask what troubles you in it, and say it to God as plainly as Abraham did when he asked, “Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?” (Genesis 18:25). Do not settle for an answer that costs you nothing. Then notice the warning Joshua gave his own people. Ask what you are tempted to take for yourself out of something that belongs to God.

passages.t: Rahab brought out, and the city burned
passages.happening:
While the city is falling, Joshua sends the two scouts to keep their oath. “Go into the house of the prostitute and bring out the woman and all who are with her, just as you promised her” (verse 22).

They bring out Rahab, her father and mother, her brothers, and all who belong to her, and settle them outside the camp of Israel (verse 23).

The city is burned. The silver and gold and the vessels of bronze and iron are put into the treasury of the LORD's house (verse 24).

Then the writer says what became of her. “And Joshua spared Rahab the prostitute, with her father’s household and all who belonged to her, because she hid the men Joshua had sent to spy out Jericho. So she has lived among the Israelites to this day” (verse 25).

Joshua lays a curse on anyone who rebuilds Jericho. Such a man will lay its foundations at the cost of his firstborn and set up its gates at the cost of his youngest (verse 26).

“So the LORD was with Joshua, and his fame spread throughout the land” (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
The writer frames the fall of Jericho with Rahab. Her name comes just before the wall falls and again just after. The last picture the chapter leaves is not only a burned city. It is a Canaanite family, alive, among the people of Israel.

Israel kept its word. The oath had been sworn by two scouts to a woman of an enemy city, in a single night, with no witness but God. In the noise of a falling city it would have been easy to forget. Joshua sends the very men who swore it.

Her family is first settled ‘outside the camp’. The camp of Israel, with the ark at its center, was kept as a holy place. The verse that follows shows where the story ends. Rahab did not stay at the edge. She ‘lived among the Israelites’. The words ‘to this day’ mean that when this was written, her family could still be pointed to.

The curse on Jericho seems to concern rebuilding it as a walled city, with foundations and gates. The place itself was not left empty. Later books mention people living there.

The last verse answers the first chapter. God had promised to be with Joshua as he had been with Moses, and the writer now says that he was.
passages.later:
The curse is taken up centuries later, in the days of King Ahab: “Hiel the Bethelite rebuilt Jericho. At the cost of Abiram his firstborn he laid its foundation, and at the cost of Segub his youngest he set up its gates, according to the word that the LORD had spoken through Joshua son of Nun” (1 Kings 16:34).

Rahab's story goes on much further. Matthew names her in the family line of Jesus: “Salmon was the father of Boaz by Rahab” (Matthew 1:5). Hebrews honors her faith: “By faith the prostitute Rahab, because she welcomed the spies in peace, did not perish with those who were disobedient” (Hebrews 11:31).
passages.asks: The scouts were sent back into a burning city to keep a promise made to a foreigner. Ask what promise you have made that would be easy to forget now that things have moved on. And think of Rahab, first set outside the camp and then living among the people. Ask who is at the edge of your church or your table, and what it would take for them to live among you.
